drills.q: A colleague says 'we deployed on SageMaker, it costs $X/month.' What's your first clarifying question and why does it matter?
drills.a: Which inference mode -- real-time endpoint, Serverless Inference, Async Inference, or Batch Transform. Each has a fundamentally different billing shape (per instance-hour 24/7, per invocation with scale-to-zero, per invocation with scale-to-zero and queuing, or per offline job) so 'SageMaker costs $X' is meaningless without knowing which of the four is being billed.

drills.q: Why can't you serve a fine-tuned Bedrock model on-demand?
drills.a: Bedrock requires Provisioned Throughput for any custom fine-tuned model -- on-demand pricing is only available for the base foundation models AWS hosts at shared capacity. This changes the cost model of fine-tuning: even a lightly-used fine-tuned model commits you to a flat hourly model-unit rate, not pay-per-token.

drills.q: Your team ran the numbers and self-hosting vLLM 'saves 60% vs Bedrock' based on GPU-hour cost alone. What's missing from that analysis?
drills.a: Engineer-hours for ongoing operation -- monitoring, patching, incident response, and model updates for a production self-hosted fleet are commonly estimated at 10-20 hours/month minimum at $75-150/hour, adding $750-3,000/month that a pure GPU-hour comparison omits. Redo the comparison with a realistic labor line item before committing to the migration; the naive comparison very often erases most or all of the claimed savings at low-to-medium volume.

drills.q: Design the inference architecture for a 200-page PDF summarization pipeline with a same-business-day SLA and bursty arrival. Which SageMaker/Bedrock components and why not a real-time endpoint?
drills.a: Textract (matched to the actual document structure) for OCR into S3, then either SageMaker Async Inference (self-hosted model, large payload, no strict latency need) or Bedrock on-demand (foundation model) triggered by a queue. A real-time endpoint would bill per instance-hour 24/7 regardless of whether a document is actively being processed -- the wrong cost shape for bursty, non-latency-critical traffic where idle capacity between bursts would be pure waste.

drills.q: A team wants 'a RAG system' but hasn't decided between Kendra, OpenSearch, and Bedrock Knowledge Bases. What's the one question that resolves it fastest?
drills.a: Is the product a search experience for humans (with access control, connectors to SharePoint/Confluence/etc., a UI) or is it purely 'feed an LLM good context'? If the former, Kendra. If the latter and the team wants zero index ops, Bedrock Knowledge Bases. If the latter but retrieval quality needs custom tuning (chunking strategy, hybrid BM25+vector scoring, a specific reranker), direct OpenSearch.

drills.q: Your Textract bill is dominated by AnalyzeExpense calls but investigation shows most input documents are plain-text internal memos, not invoices. What happened and what's the fix?
drills.a: The pipeline is calling the wrong API for the document type -- AnalyzeExpense is priced for structured invoice/receipt field extraction (~$10/1,000 pages) when DetectDocumentText (~$1.50/1,000 pages) would suffice for plain text, a roughly 6-7x avoidable cost difference on this subset alone. Fix: classify document type first (even a cheap heuristic or Comprehend custom classifier) and route to the cheapest Textract API that satisfies the actual extraction need.

drills.q: A SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint shows latency spikes correlated with periods of low traffic, not with request complexity. Diagnose and give two possible fixes with their tradeoffs.
drills.a: Cold starts -- Serverless Inference scales to zero when idle and pays a provisioning penalty on the next invocation after a gap. Fix 1: switch to a real-time endpoint, eliminating cold starts entirely but paying for capacity 24/7 even during genuinely idle periods -- only worth it if traffic volume is high enough that idle cost is small relative to total cost. Fix 2: if available for the workload, use Provisioned Concurrency for Serverless Inference to keep some capacity warm without going fully real-time -- a middle ground that still has a cost for the warm capacity reserved.

drills.q: Explain why 'self-hosting is cheaper above 11B tokens/month' and 'self-hosting is cheaper above 100M tokens/month' can both appear as cited figures without either being wrong.
drills.a: They come from different underlying assumptions -- which frontier model's on-demand price is the baseline, whether GPU utilization is assumed high (e.g. >60%) or conservative, and critically whether engineer-labor cost is included in the self-hosting side. A comparison against an expensive frontier model with optimistic GPU utilization and no labor cost produces a much lower break-even than one against a cheaper model with realistic utilization and a labor line item. The lesson: never quote a break-even number without also stating its assumptions, and always re-derive it for the specific case rather than reusing someone else's snapshot.

drills.q: A team building a new agent wants to know if they should use AgentCore or their existing hand-rolled LangGraph-on-EKS deployment. What's the actual decision framework, not just 'AgentCore is newer so it's better'?
drills.a: Identify what specific undifferentiated infrastructure the current LangGraph deployment has already built (session isolation, identity/auth for tools, persistent memory, observability) versus what it's missing or fragile on. If the existing stack already solves these well and is stable, migrating purely because AgentCore exists adds risk (it's new, GA mid-2026, opinionated about its execution model) for uncertain benefit. If the team is actively fighting to build session isolation or observability themselves and it's slowing feature work, AgentCore's managed runtime is solving exactly that gap and is worth evaluating concretely against the specific pain points, not adopted wholesale on reputation.

drills.q: Why does SageMaker Feature Store matter for a team already using PySpark/EMR to compute features for training?
drills.a: Without it, training-time feature computation (batch, in Spark/EMR) and serving-time feature computation (often a separate, hand-written low-latency path) can silently diverge -- different code paths computing 'the same' feature slightly differently is a classic and hard-to-detect cause of training/serving skew that degrades a model in production without any obvious error. Feature Store gives one feature definition with both an offline store (for bulk training reads) and an online store (for low-latency serving lookups), closing that gap structurally rather than relying on two implementations staying in sync by discipline.
